idiom_name: public synchronized blocks + private unsynchronized implementation methods
implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM monitor: AnyRef.synchronized runs its body under the receiver's reentrant monitor, so a component whose methods call each other does not self-deadlock and the pattern reduces to the minimal-locking-overhead discipline - one acquisition per public entry, hold count 1, an explicit critical section. Put the synchronized block in the public method, forward to private methods that assume the monitor is held, and prefer a dedicated private lock object over this.synchronized. For contention-heavy components java.util.concurrent collections, AtomicReference/AtomicInteger, or an actor/effect-system that owns the state replace the classic structure entirely; Futures are the trap, because blocking on one while holding the monitor freezes the pool.
pitfalls: The monitor is reentrant, so nested acquisition is silent - a helper that calls a public synchronized method only inflates the hold count.
synchronized on this exposes the monitor to any collaborator holding a reference; lock a private object instead.
Blocking on a Future (Await.result/Await.ready) while holding the monitor deadlocks the thread pool; a callback that re-enters the component while the monitor is held can invert lock order.
Suspending in the middle of a critical section and resuming on another thread is invisible to the monitor, so one logical operation must not be split across asynchronous boundaries.
